facts.fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
facts.hook: a first-time camper reads the camp's history plaque and learns camps are older than she thought

facts.fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
facts.hook: a camper notices an accreditation sign at the camp gate and asks a counselor what it means

facts.fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
facts.hook: a camper who thinks he is the only one missing home finds out his bunkmates feel it too

facts.fact: A 2007 American Academy of Pediatrics report advised parents not to make a 'pick-up deal', a promise to fetch a homesick child early, because it can undermine the child's confidence in coping.
facts.hook: a camper remembers her parents saying they believed she could handle a week away

facts.fact: The first known published recipe for s'mores, called 'Some More', appeared in the 1927 Girl Scouts book 'Tramping and Trailing with the Girl Scouts'.
facts.hook: an argument around the campfire over who invented s'mores

facts.fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
facts.hook: a cabin group thinks their fire is out until a counselor has them check for heat

facts.fact: Poison ivy's itchy rash is caused by urushiol, an oil in the plant, and campers remember how to spot the plant's three leaflets with the saying 'leaves of three, let it be.'
facts.hook: a camper about to grab a vine for a fort stops when a friend counts its leaves

facts.fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
facts.hook: a nightly tick check in the cabin that one camper wants to skip

facts.fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
facts.hook: a camper sunburned after a long afternoon at the lake despite putting sunscreen on that morning

facts.fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
facts.hook: a first-timer in a life jacket learns why the canoe wobbled when he stepped on its edge

facts.fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
facts.hook: campers lying on the dock at night try to find north without a phone

facts.fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
facts.hook: a camper who wandered off at swim time realizes why her buddy looked so worried

facts.fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
facts.hook: a kid notices fewer people buying lemonade after his sister doubles the price

facts.fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
facts.hook: more neighbors start selling homemade bracelets after one friend's sell out at a high price

facts.fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
facts.hook: a garage sale where the seller keeps adjusting a price until the last item sells

facts.fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
facts.hook: cheap concert tickets vanish in minutes and hundreds of fans get nothing

facts.fact: When a price is set above what buyers will pay, unsold goods pile up in what economists call a surplus, and sellers often cut prices to clear it.
facts.hook: at the end of a garage sale, everything left gets marked down to a dollar

facts.fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
facts.hook: strawberries at the farmers' market cost half what they did a month earlier

facts.fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
facts.hook: a family switches snacks at the store when their usual brand's price jumps

facts.fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why people keep buying something no matter how much its price goes up

facts.fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
facts.hook: a student asks why a bottle of water costs so little compared to a tiny gem

facts.fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
facts.hook: two friends arguing whether buyers or sellers decide a price are both right

facts.fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
facts.hook: a kid at the gas station asks why the price changed since last week

facts.fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
facts.hook: a trading-card craze at school ends as suddenly as it started

facts.fact: As a sophomore at Laney High School in North Carolina, Michael Jordan tried out for the varsity basketball team but was judged too short, at 5 feet 11 inches, and played junior varsity instead.
facts.hook: a player who did not make the team wonders whether to try again next year

facts.fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
facts.hook: a player born in December realizes most of the kids who made the team are months older

facts.fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
facts.hook: a runner at tryouts has to decide whether to sprint early or pace herself

facts.fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
facts.hook: a player who felt fine after day one of tryouts can barely climb stairs on day two

facts.fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
facts.hook: a girl trying out for a team learns why her school must offer girls' sports

facts.fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
facts.hook: a player hits his head during tryouts and wants to keep going so he doesn't miss his chance

facts.fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
facts.hook: a coach pulls a player from the tryout after a hard fall, and the player learns it is the law

facts.fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
facts.hook: a player stays up late gaming the night before tryouts and feels slow the next day

facts.fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
facts.hook: a swimmer forgets her water bottle and fades in the last heat of tryouts

facts.fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
facts.hook: a nervous player skips the warm-up to watch the others and regrets it

facts.fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
facts.hook: a player shows up to tryouts without the signed physical form

facts.fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
facts.hook: a swimmer's time from a bigger pool can't be compared directly with her tryout time

facts.fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
facts.hook: a new volunteer reads the food bank's history on the break-room wall

facts.fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
facts.hook: a volunteer asks how long food banks have existed in her country

facts.fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
facts.hook: a first-time volunteer is surprised there are no customers at the warehouse

facts.fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
facts.hook: a volunteer notices the same logo on trucks from different cities

facts.fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
facts.hook: a sorter is about to throw out cereal one day past its date

facts.fact: Food safety agencies advise throwing away cans that are bulging, leaking, or deeply dented, especially along a seam, so food bank sorters set such cans aside.
facts.hook: a volunteer finds a swollen can in a donation bin and asks what to do

facts.fact: The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.
facts.hook: a volunteer sees a grocery store's donated produce and wonders how much food never gets eaten

facts.fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
facts.hook: a Saturday picking leftover potatoes from a farmer's field

facts.fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
facts.hook: a volunteer's grandparent recognizes the idea from an old story

facts.fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
facts.hook: a volunteer stacks new cans in front and gets asked to redo the shelf

facts.fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
facts.hook: a class signs up to volunteer on a school holiday in January

facts.fact: In the United States, the USDA defines food insecurity as a household lacking consistent access to enough food for an active, healthy life.
facts.hook: a volunteer learns that a classmate's family sometimes visits the pantry

facts.fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
facts.hook: a grandparent at the watch party claims to remember the very first one

facts.fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
facts.hook: a kid asks why the big game uses Roman numerals

facts.fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
facts.hook: a family argues over which country won the first World Cup

facts.fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
facts.hook: fans at a playoff watch party wonder why the trophy looks so old

facts.fact: The names of many players, coaches, and staff from each Stanley Cup-winning team are engraved on the Cup's bands.
facts.hook: a kid dreams aloud of seeing her name on the trophy one day

facts.fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
facts.hook: a disputed call gets replayed and a relative says TV once couldn't do that

facts.fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
facts.hook: a cousin from another country calls the wave by a different name

facts.fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
facts.hook: friends argue whether their team only won because it played at home

facts.fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
facts.hook: a fan wonders whether cheering at the stadium really helps the team

facts.fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
facts.hook: a kid asks why no player on TV wears number 42

facts.fact: Every April 15 since 2004, Major League Baseball celebrates Jackie Robinson Day, when every player on every team wears the number 42.
facts.hook: a family turns on a game and every player's jersey shows the same number

facts.fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
facts.hook: during a timeout, a kid wonders why it's called a basket
